Before writing any review, I wanted to finish the game properly. And that took me over 150 hours; 150 absolutely AMAZING hours of adventure, filled with unforgettable moments and so many positive emotions.

When I first started playing and got into my first battle, I wasn't exactly impressed. The turn-based combat system didn't convince me at all. I guess nostalgia for the good old combat system from Baldur's Gate 1 and 2 was simply too strong. But I decided to give it a chance, and once I got used to it, I realised it actually adds a whole new dimension to the game.

The same goes for the party size. Having only four characters instead of the six we had in BG1 and BG2 was initially a bit disappointing. Again, nostalgia talking. But after spending some time with the game, I realised just how brilliantly balanced the four-character party actually is. It adds another layer of complexity, forces you to think more tactically, make better use of every character's abilities, and really get the most out of your party.

And then there's everything else... The depth of the game. The seemingly endless possibilities. The decisions and their consequences. The dialogue. The incredible characters and their personal stories.

And this is where the game truly shines. Every major character you meet, especially your companions, has an incredibly detailed story of their own, one you can gradually uncover and become deeply involved in. But what makes it so special is that you're not just watching their stories unfold. You're actively shaping them. Depending on your choices, their personalities, relationships, beliefs and ultimately their fates can change dramatically. Who they become and where their stories lead is, to a remarkable extent, in your hands.

And those decisions don't exist in isolation. They have consequences, sometimes immediate, sometimes much later when you least expect them. They shape your companions, your relationships, the dynamics of your party and ultimately your entire gameplay experience. It's this incredible sense that your choices genuinely matter that makes the world feel so alive and every playthrough so personal. And, of course, a wonderful dose of nostalgia when Jaheira and Minsc showed up. Seeing those two again was something special... #corememoriesunlocked. :)

To spare you another essay, I'll get straight to the point:  This game, without a single doubt, is the best RPG I've ever played and easily among my top three games of all time. And the best part? After finishing my first playthrough, I'm already excited about what comes next. Honour Mode, different origin characters, different choices, different approaches, and all the things I haven't even discovered yet. 
In fact, I've already started my second playthrough. And despite knowing that the main storyline remains the same, thanks to the incredible variety of possibilities, it already feels like I'm playing an entirely new game.

So here's to another 150, 300, or even 500 hours of adventure. And somehow, I have a feeling even that might not be enough. :) AN ABSOLUTE MASTERPIECE!!! 100/10!

I put off playing Baldur's Gate 3 for years because I didn't believe it could possibly live up to the hype. All I'd seen from it were clips of dialogue or exploits. I didn't expect it at all to be the most unique RPG I've ever played for one reason that stands out above all others: the sheer flexibility. Many single-player RPGs either don't allow you to bend the rules or the narrative, while others let you bend them so far that they break. Baldur's Gate 3 lets you bend every quest to the point where you expect it to break, but it never does. I cannot emphasise enough just how much the game accounts for every action you could possibly choose to take in every situation, so I'm not going to try.

An aspect I hadn't seen much (if any) of was the combat, so I had no idea what to expect. I'm coming at this as someone who has zero experience with D&D mechanics. I very wrongly assumed that the inherent randomness of "dice rolls" determining every move would make the game feel random and unfun, but that's almost precisely what makes it so engaging. Your character builds all influence the bonuses your dice rolls get, so you actually have a lot of control. There are moments where you feel like the rolls are BS, but they're so rare, and they can make fights feel much more intense. Also, the fights can be LONG. I'm talking 10 minutes for basic encounters and upwards of 20 minutes for big ones.

Another expectation I had that was completely wrong was that it's an open world. The game is broken up into three "Acts", which can be anywhere from 30–60 hours each in a single run. Each act takes place on a fairly big map, but it's by no means an open world. This isn't a bad thing, and I really enjoyed exploring each area of every map to find encounters ranging from small scuffles to treasure hauls. They're very distinctly different from each other, too, so I never felt as though it was a repetitive cycle.

One thing I was slightly let down by was the fact that some builds just aren't viable long-term, so you can easily end up with characters who are frustratingly weak and others who are borderline broken, without intending any of it. Each class has multiple subclasses, and it's very intimidating at first to choose one based on its initial description, so you end up choosing something that sounds cool only to find out it sucks either in the short or long term. You can respec at any point, so it's not the end of the world, but it is a shame that I felt the classes aren't as balanced as they could be.

Without getting into spoilers, the main narrative focus of the journey you go on is more about getting to know each of the characters you end up having in your gang. The overarching goal is more of a motivator to keep the journey going rather than the main hook that will keep you invested. If I had to sum up my thoughts on each of the characters, they would be:

[spoiler]Astarion: Funny most of the time, but I found him to be too on the nose and in-your-face in terms of being a borderline villain. He has the funniest dialogue scene in the game in Act 1. I won't say what, but if you know, you know. I do like the conclusion to his quest a lot, but he feels very disconnected for most of the game.

Gale: Nerd emoji wizard. He feels more connected to the main story, and I did like having him in my party. No strong feelings towards him.

Lae'zel: Feels the most connected to the main narrative for most of the game, and is also one of the top contenders for my personal favourite. Her evolution as a character is definitely the most dramatic. I found her ignorance of the world and fight-or-die mentality very charming.

Karlach: Initially, I couldn't stand her. She talks like a modern-day, quippy millennial, and I hated it. She does have some of the most dramatic dialogue and a seemingly high-stakes story, but she doesn't have much to do for most of the game in terms of a personal story. I like her more dramatic moments, though, and she did end up growing on me.

Shadowheart: The other contender for my favourite of the gang. She is also very much tied to the main story in every act in the most significant way. Weirdly, she seems like the most normal and pragmatic of the bunch and is very easy to get along with.

Wyll: I found Wyll to be the polar opposite of Astarion, in that he's a goody-two-shoes, sometimes to an obnoxious degree. I liked his character, though, and the dilemma he finds himself in is a very cool twist for a hero-type character.
[/spoiler]

There are others who can join that I didn't mention, but they're not as deep as the main six and to be honest I didn't use them in my party so I can't comment. Each of the characters in your party reacts to your decisions in dialogue, and you actually learn a great deal about each one of them purely from the "X Approves/Disapproves" pop-up when you're in dialogue.

I honestly think Baldur's Gate 3 is a little overhyped, but that doesn't mean I don't love it. If you are a diehard RPG fan who wants the truest RPG experience possible, this is your game. Everything it tries to do, it succeeds at exceptionally well. One of the ending cutscenes is one of the most jaw-dropping things I've seen in a game. I won't say in what way.

This might be the only review you need if you are New to CRPGs or turn-based games

If CD Projekt Red gave us The Witcher 3, then Larian Studios gave us its CRPG equivalent with Baldur's Gate 3. And I mean that as one of the highest compliments possible.

I was never into turn-based combat. In fact, I avoided the entire genre because I thought it wasn't my thing. Boy, was I wrong.

The combat and mechanics can feel overwhelming at first. I actually started on the lowest difficulty because I was so invested in the role-playing that I just wanted to keep the story moving. But here's the beauty of it: the game grows with you. In Act 1, you're figuring things out. In Act 2, you're discovering mechanics you didn't even know existed. By Act 3, you're still learning new tricks. And somehow, it never stops being rewarding.

But the real magic? The freedom.

Imagine the freedom of a CRPG combined with the cinematic presentation of a AAA RPG. Fully voiced conversations, incredible cutscenes, memorable companions, and a developer that seemingly thought of EVERYTHING.

Think of a ridiculous way to solve a quest? There's probably a way to do it. Wonder what happens if you betray someone, save someone, kill someone, or simply walk away? There's probably a dialogue, consequence, or entire story branch waiting for you.

This is ROLE-PLAYING in its purest form. Your companions, decisions, relationships, and even the smallest choices can shape your journey.

And by the time the credits roll, you're not thinking about uninstalling. You're thinking:

"What if I chose differently?"

"What if I brought another companion?"

"Wait... I could've done THAT?!"

The branching possibilities are practically an Elden Tree of their own, except every branch makes you want to start another 100-hour playthrough.

If turn-based combat is the only thing stopping you from playing Baldur's Gate 3, don't let it.

I've owned Baldur's Gate for just less than a year, and the first few times I tried the game it just didn't click. However, like many other titles this year I gave it another shot, and I really loved it this time around. The combat took a little getting used to, I've played so many other RPGs that the idea of frequent long rests was foreign to me (gotta keep the loot til you roll credits), but once I got past those obstacles I could finally get into the meat on the bones.

The best part of the game is easily the cast of characters, both in your party and spread throughout the world. Whilst at first very few of them really appealed to me, by the end of the game I loved almost every last one of them. Astarion, a character I heavily disliked initially, somehow ended up being my favourite character by the time I rolled credits - the writing is just really good when it comes to their development (depending on your choices, I'd assume), and of course the incredible voice acting only does further wonders (looking at you Samantha Béart). Of course, there's a few instances where dialogue doesn't account for some situations, and it can take you out of it (e.g., Astarion and Gale would pretend like they helped defeat the goblin camp in Act 1, yet I hadn't even recruited them until I was on my way back to the grove), but that's a small nitpick.

The story, whilst nothing special, is the perfect vessel for giving you both these incredible characters and their individual quest lines, and also allows for so much freedom of choice. It's truly remarkable how much you can truly unlock or miss all dependent on your choices and attributes. Of course, sometimes it might be frustrating to fail a roll and miss something, but once you get used to it you can really start enjoying it more. Save scumming is of course an option (though sometimes the terrible autosave is enough), but I found that it really just disrupts the flow of the game and I only ever used it if I was really getting sick of a quest.

As previously mentioned, the combat is quite fun but has a learning curve for sure. Spell slots and healing are all things that take some getting used to whilst you learn to rely more on short and long rests, but by the halfway point of act 1 you'll likely get the hang of it. That said, the combat does falter heavily in act 3, where encounters become these bloated hoards of enemies which are more frustrating than they are challenging, with lots of mechanics which just generally aren't fun to fight against no matter the build. It really takes you out of it, which isn't helped by the broken enemy AI you will typically encounter at this stage of the game - where enemies (including bosses) will freeze up and not do anything, dragging out fights and just ruining the moment completely.

There is one final complaint, and this one is the major one for me, but the autosaves just aren't good. It's too infrequent, and you will often find yourself loading a save about an hour old or longer when your party dies. It's frustrating, ruins the flow, and makes you care less and less about the quest you're doing. And boy did this happen a lot. F5 will be your most pressed key by the time credits roll, that I can assure you. You might also think you can save yourself the trouble by downloading an autosave improvement mod, but then you lose access to your achievements - which is a stupid rule for such a minor QoL mod, and I hate it every time games that do this, Cyberpunk now included as of update 2.5.

Despite my long rants about what I disliked, the game does offer so much that I really do recommend - a beautiful world full of so many interesting and unique characters, with thousands of possible ways to make your next play through different from the last.

I am tempted to write a much longer review but I suspect everyone who will ever care already knows what a sublime masterful game this is, so I will suffice it to say that if there ever was an RPG worth playing all the way through, worth sinking thousands of hours into, worth experimenting with different gameplay styles and going for all the achievements and playing through the game a hundred times with all the difficulty settings, worth trying out the plethora of mods to make the game even spicier after you think you've seen all there is to see in the vanilla game (you haven't), worth losing your free time, your family time, your work time, your job, your house, your wife and kids in the settlement, losing all but your PC and maybe a hijacked power connection from your local Denny's- it's Baldur's Gate 3.

Yes I think I would recommend it.

I was going through my history of games I've played but never reviewed, and I honestly couldn't believe I never wrote anything about Baldur's Gate 3. I don't even know where to begin with this game. I genuinely can't put into words just how amazing the entire experience was.

The story, the gameplay, the characters, the world, the music, the exploration. Everything. It's one of those rare games where everything just comes together to create something truly special.

The amount of freedom you're given is incredible. Your choices actually matter, the world reacts to your decisions, and there are so many different ways to approach situations that it almost feels impossible to experience everything in a single playthrough. The writing is phenomenal, and the companions feel like actual people with their own personalities, struggles, and motivations. You genuinely become attached to them.

The combat is fantastic, too. Every encounter feels like a puzzle with multiple solutions, and the game constantly rewards creativity and experimentation. Even after spending countless hours playing, I was still discovering new things.

But what really sets Baldur's Gate 3 apart is how it makes you feel.

It's one of those games where, when the credits finally roll, you almost feel depressed because it's over. You've spent so much time in this world, getting to know these characters, making decisions, fighting battles, and experiencing this incredible adventure. And then suddenly, it's done. You sit there staring at the screen, not knowing what to do with yourself or what game could possibly come next.

Very few games have ever left me with that feeling. It's almost like saying goodbye to a group of friends after an unforgettable journey.

As much as I want to jump back in and experience it all over again, I'm actually going to give it a few years before I replay it. I want to forget as much as I can about the story, the characters, and all those little moments that made the game so special. I know I'll never be able to experience it for the first time again, but maybe if I give it enough time, some of those memories will fade just enough that I can rediscover a little of that magic. That's how much this game meant to me.

I could probably write pages about everything I loved, and it still wouldn't do the game justice.

Baldur's Gate 3 isn't just one of the best RPGs I've ever played. It's one of the greatest games I've ever experienced, period. I wish I could erase my memory of it just to experience it all over again for the first time.

I was gifted this game from my bestie for my birthday after she let me try playing a bit back in college. I've never played any of the Baldur's Gate games prior to this one nor had I played DnD at the time, but my friend and I both play MTG and they have a lot of crossover. The first time I played BG3, I had no idea what to expect beyond the beach and the Illithid crash site but like in Fallout 3/4, I spent a majority of the time I borrowed my friend's game in the character creator. I had never seen something so complex and details besides the Sims 3 when it came down to minute details and such from character background to physical aspects and you can imagine my surprise when I was asked what junk I wanted! The diversity reminded me of a more explicit TS3 character experience. I was recommended Story Mode to start and I think that's best for someone brand new to these types of games. I made my little female Tiefling Druid a Mephistopheles worshipper and I think it's kinda funny how I had no idea how important these aspects would be not just at the start of the game, but throughout all 3 Acts! After that first playthrough where everyone made it out to the party sans Gale as I played completely blind and acted as if I was myself. That ended in me romancing Lae'zel and us fighting among the cosmos with me sacrificing myself to become a Mindflayer. She didn't care and neither did others considering I was the hero who saved everyone. I like to think there was still a little piece of me somewhere in there and hope that Omellum faced less prejudice and fear of being out in public. My second full playthrough as a female Drow Durge let me go crazy. I did everything I could possibly do to impress my dad. I naively thought Minthara and I could rule together but alas, I killed everyone and their mother much to my father's approval. I watched all the endings to see what would happen if I made different choices at the very end like betraying my father, stabbing Minthy and quickly going after the others in my party. Even Ascended Astarion stood no chance...my first choice picked though was my human heart feeling bad and warning my party that they can run but in the end, I will come and kill them last. Now I am on my third full run and am playing as a goody two shoes male elf of nobility as I wanted to romance our favorite vampire, but he hates me and will likely leave my party soon as I've received a couple warnings now, but as for who I'm romancing? Gale. This time, he won't die. I love this game and have watched hours of lore and re-imaginings  and am going to start a run as a male Drow looking to escape Menzobarranzan...looks like he's going to get his wish with a caveat! My next run will be an Oathbreaker (from the sounds of it...it's very easy to do) but on one of the higher difficulties as I've chosen normal difficulty for Durge and the elf and have the mechanics down pretty well. If there's one thing I wish was in the game, it's that we get more Omellum. It is my favorite NPC with an unfortunately little amount of content.
